hints: Look at the starting molecule, 2-bromopropane is a halogenoalkane, so think about what kind of reagent water or hydroxide is.
Notice that the Br atom is replaced by an OH group to form propan-2-ol, so one group swaps for another.
Decide if this swapping by an electron-rich species is an addition or a substitution, and whether the attacker is a nucleophile or electrophile.
walkthrough:
**Identify the starting material**

Great start, 2-bromopropane is a halogenoalkane with formula $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_3$. The C-Br bond is polar, with carbon slightly positive, so it attracts electron-rich species.

Structure:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_3$$

**Identify what hydrolysis does**

Hydrolysis means reaction with water or aqueous $\text{OH}^-$ to replace the halogen with an OH group. Here we make propan-2-ol.

Overall change:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_3 + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_3 + \text{Br}^-$$

**Classify the mechanism type**

One group ($\text{Br}$) leaves and another ($\text{OH}$) takes its place, so this is substitution, not addition. The attacker $\text{OH}^-$ or $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ donates a pair of electrons to carbon, so it is a nucleophile. Put together, this is nucleophilic substitution.

options.A: Electrophilic addition happens to alkenes when an electrophile attacks the C=C double bond. 2-bromopropane is saturated with no double bond, so nothing can add across it.
options.B: Free radical substitution needs radicals and usually UV light, as in methane with chlorine. Hydrolysis uses polar nucleophiles like water or OH-, not radicals, so this does not fit.
options.C: Nucleophilic addition happens to carbonyl compounds like aldehydes and ketones where a nucleophile adds to the C=O without anything leaving. Here a Br leaves and OH replaces it, so it is substitution, not addition.
options.D: Correct and well done. The nucleophile $\text{OH}^-$ (or $\text{H}_2\text{O}$) attacks the electron-deficient carbon and substitutes $\text{Br}^-$ to give propan-2-ol. This is the classic hydrolysis of a halogenoalkane by nucleophilic substitution.
